analysis.one_liner: Limits electric utilities to requesting one retail rate increase per year.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no hearing or vote since its introduction day in September 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a rule to a 1978 law that requires states to consider standards for electric utilities, telling states to weigh a limit under which a utility can ask for only one retail rate increase every 365 days [S2]. Utilities commonly file rate cases multiple times in a year to recover costs and boost returns; a once-a-year cap would slow that cadence. The measure was introduced by Rep. Josh Harder with three Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, where no further action has been taken [S1][S3][S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Electric ratepayers, especially households facing repeated utility bill increases. Limiting how often utilities can file for rate increases would give families more predictable bills and state regulators more breathing room between rate cases. It would also reduce utilities' ability to seek frequent, incremental increases that individually draw less scrutiny.

how_it_helps.text: Adds a standard to the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act of 1978 under which each electric utility may request no more than one rate increase once per year [S2].
Requires states to consider adopting this cap as part of the standards process the 1978 law already mandates [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Investor-owned electric utilities, which would face a slower path to recovering costs and earning returns through frequent rate filings. In theory, if a utility cannot file often, it may bundle larger requests into a single annual increase, which could produce bigger one-time jumps even if the total number of filings falls.

drawbacks.text: A cap on frequency does not cap rates. A utility could respond by asking for one very large increase per year instead of several smaller ones, so total bills might not fall [S2].

The text as drafted says each electric utility 'shall request no more than one rate increase once per year' [S2], while the underlying law generally treats these standards as items states must consider adopting, not direct federal mandates, so the practical effect depends entirely on whether states choose to implement it.
Slowing rate filings could delay a utility's recovery of sudden cost spikes, such as fuel price surges, which in a worst case could strain a utility's finances or push costs onto future bills.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ratepayers, the benefit is predictability and less piecemeal rate creep, but the bill does not limit how much rates can rise in any single increase, so its real-world savings are uncertain. For utilities, the cost is reduced flexibility, which is modest. The biggest weakness is design: it addresses how often rates go up rather than how much, leaving the core affordability question open.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the same day in September 2025 and has not moved since; with the current Congress running into early 2027, it technically remains alive but inactive [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Josh Harder introduced the bill on September 4, 2025 [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce that same day, the only action taken since introduction [S4].
Three Democratic colleagues cosponsored the bill [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, utilities are better off because no restriction has advanced, while ratepayers get no relief either way since nothing has been enacted. The bill's inaction reflects its narrow cosponsor base, not an active campaign against it on the record.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities so far; ratepayers get nothing yet

for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill at introduction

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over utility regulation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action - no hearing, markup, or floor scheduling - in the months since

sides.party_line_note: All four initial supporters, including the sponsor, are Democrats; no Republican cosponsors have joined, and no votes have occurred to show a broader split.

industries.note: The bill would limit these utilities to one retail rate increase request per year, slowing their ability to recover costs and raise returns through frequent filings. Because utilities profit by charging customers more, their interest here runs against ratepayers' [S2].
Regulators would gain a new standard to consider that could simplify their workload by spacing out rate cases, but they would also face federal direction on how to run their process.

analysis.trajectory: With only three cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee activity more than a month after referral, the bill is unlikely to receive a hearing or vote in the current Congress. Most bills at this stage die in committee, and this one shows none of the early signals - a markup, a hearing, or broadening sponsorship - that typically precede action.
